prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map separates a near seating area from a farther raised walkway and glass wall: in frame 1, chairs and the couch occupy the left foreground/midground at roughly 1–3 m, while the standing person near the upper-right walkway is about 4–6 m away. Across frames 2–4, a person passes extremely close in front of the camera, approximately 0.3–1 m away, first on the right and then filling much of the centre/right; this person occludes the couch, walkway, and much of the room, while the farther standing person remains roughly 3–5 m away and above the camera wearer because of the raised floor. By frame 5 the near person has moved out of view, revealing chairs and plants about 1–3 m ahead/right and the more distant room surfaces; the nearby furniture is within or near arm's reach only at the closest edges. Brightness makes the close person's silhouette and the foreground floor easier to separate than in RGB, but the nearly uniform bright wall/floor regions, dark distant areas, blurred boundaries, and apparent depth discontinuities around people and furniture make precise distances and relative spacing unreliable.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map identifies a couch and several chairs clustered on the left in frame 1, with potted plants above/behind them and a person farther right; the furniture cluster spans roughly 1–3 m from the camera, while that person is about 4–6 m away. In frames 2–4, two person instances are separated: one farther person remains near the raised walkway, while a second person moves very close across the foreground, enlarging until the mask fills much of the right side and blocks the couch and background; the two people appear several metres apart. Frame 4 also isolates a chair in the lower-right foreground, roughly 1–2 m away, and frame 5 shows chairs and potted plants along the right side, including objects partly cut off by the image boundary. The masks reveal object identity and occlusion more clearly than RGB, but they omit much of the floor, walls, tables, and glass structure, fragment or miss small objects, and provide no dependable body orientation or metric distance by themselves.
descriptions.pose: The pose map detects one upright body near the centre-left in frame 2 at roughly 3–5 m, positioned on the raised walkway above and behind the nearer foreground person visible in RGB; the skeleton's side-biased profile suggests the person is oriented mostly across the scene rather than directly toward the camera. In frame 3, only a small, tilted upper-body or limb cluster is detected near the upper centre at a similar background location, so facing direction and gaze toward the camera cannot be established reliably. No usable skeleton is shown for the person passing within roughly 0.3–1 m of the camera, likely because that person is heavily cropped and occludes the view, and no people are detected in frames 1, 4, or 5 despite partial figures being visible in RGB. The map makes articulated body location and upright posture clearer than RGB where detection succeeds, but missing joints, the malformed frame-3 skeleton, absent hand detections, and lack of facial landmarks make reach, gaze, and precise orientation highly unreliable.
